title: The first financial AI benchmark that is actually useful
author: Felixdaga1
selftext:
While building my own trading agent, I noticed how little resources/guides are out there; Which model/harness is actually better at trading? What are their biases and blindspots? What should I look out for? 

The current financial AI benchmarks like [AA financial index](https://artificialanalysis.ai/models/capabilities/finance-and-accounting) are suppose to help but they only score the model on generic financial tasks or questions, not investment performance or the agentic system as a whole. Moreover, they are designed by the AI builders who 1) have no proper investment experience or 2) have incentive to promote their products. 

So I saw the need for a financial AI benchmark done by those who are actually investing with AI. Long story short I had to re-imagine how an "AI investment benchmark" should be done and develop an eval pipeline to implement it. Turns out if you run enough time-controlled simulations (aka backtesting the AI), you could really understand their performance and traits at a whole new level - their expected performance (based on your strategy), factor/sector biases or even down to how the harness is affecting the stocks they pick. Essentially I am generating a **resume for each agent** I'm testing.

I'm just starting to publish the results [here](https://www.fintel.capital/scoreboard).

Funding it out of my own pocket atm (it could cost > 100$ per run just to get enough data) but I believe it could help the next person trying to invest with AI like I did. So pls comment on your thoughts or suggest a harness-model combo I could try next, thinking hermes?

Peace out!

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
The thing I would want in the resume before the model name is the spread across repeated runs of the same combo. Same prompts, same window, different sampling, and the picks diverge enough that one run per combo is ranking noise rather than models. Report a band instead of a point and a lot of the apparent gaps between harnesses close, and whichever ones survive that are the actual finding.

Since you are funding it yourself, that is also the cheapest place to spend: how many runs per combo are you doing now, and is temperature pinned across them?

replies.author: Felixdaga1
replies.body:
ahh yes to account for LLM stochasticity. I have only done 1 run per combo so far for the public results. The 100$ is purely from backtesting the AI agent once - across 17 periods and 30 tickers per agent. I plan to do 3-5 repeats going forward, at least for the cheaper models.  
  
This is different from the usual financial benchmarks where models are just answering questions so they can afford to repeat it many times. But I have done previous studies on this if ur interested - [https://felixdaga.github.io/Optimized\_Agent/posts/2026-07-16-optimizing-ai-agents-for-alpha-generation/](https://felixdaga.github.io/Optimized_Agent/posts/2026-07-16-optimizing-ai-agents-for-alpha-generation/)

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
Running an agent across 17 periods and 30 tickers is a different cost class than a Q&A benchmark, so one run per combo is a fair place to start. Once you have 3 to 5, worth reporting the spread across repeats rather than the mean, since the spread is the finding.

Are you fixing seed and temperature, or letting both float?
